claims.text: Arc melting on a water-cooled Cu hearth provides rapid quenching that can stabilize a dual-phase microstructure in FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys.
The stabilized dual-phase microstructure increases coercivity relative to conventional single-phase fcc alloys.
Nominally equiatomic FeCoNiTi in the as-cast state contains coexisting fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves phases.
Rapid quenching locks in the dual-phase fcc+C14 microstructure.
Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29 is a C14-dominant comparison variant.
The fcc phase has an approximate composition of Fe21.3Co24.8Ni32.2Ti21.6.
The C14 phase has an approximate composition of Fe27.3Co26.6Ni17.4Ti28.7.
Antiferromagnetic coupling occurs between the Fe/Co/Ni sublattice and the Ti sublattice.
This antiferromagnetic sublattice coupling reduces saturation magnetization.
The fcc phase exhibits high-temperature ferromagnetic ordering at approximately 1084 K.
Interfaces with the C14 phase enhance an induced orbital moment in the fcc phase.
The enhanced orbital moment and spin canting improve domain-wall pinning.
Dual-phase FeCoNiTi may reach a coercive field of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloys typically have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy should show multiple magnetic transitions, including transitions near 168 K and 1084 K attributed to the fcc phase.
The coercivity enhancement depends critically on coexistence and interfacial interactions between the fcc and C14 phases.
Fully single-phase fcc or single-phase C14 alloys should not show the same coercivity enhancement or distinct multiple magnetic-ordering transitions.

contradictions.description: Magnetic measurements are limited to 400 K, but the hypothesis predicts and uses the presence or absence of a transition near 1084 K as an observable discriminator. That transition cannot be tested over the stated measurement range.
